hints: Recall that amount in moles equals concentration times volume in dm3, so first convert the titre volume from cm3 to dm3 by dividing by 1000.
walkthrough:
Set up the moles formula for a solution**
Think of concentration as moles packed into each $\text{dm}^{3}$. So moles = concentration $\times$ volume in $\text{dm}^{3}$. Here $c = 0.0200 \, \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and $V = 27.30 \, \text{cm}^{3}$.

Convert and substitute**
Convert to $\text{dm}^{3}$: $$V = \frac{27.30}{1000} = 0.02730 \, \text{dm}^{3}$$ Then: $$n(\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}) = 0.0200 \times 0.02730 = 5.46 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{mol}$$

hints: Look at the given ionic equation and compare the coefficients of $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to find how many moles of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ react with one mole of dichromate.
walkthrough:
Read the ratio from the balanced ionic equation**
The equation shows: $$\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-} + 14\text{H}^{+} + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ One mole of $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ oxidises six moles of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$. So the ratio is $1:6$.

Scale up your answer from (i)**
$$n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 6 \times 5.46 \times 10^{-4} = 3.276 \times 10^{-3} \approx 3.28 \times 10^{-3} \, \text{mol}$$ This is the amount in the $25.0 \, \text{cm}^{3}$ pipetted sample.

hints: Remember the $25.0 \, \text{cm}^{3}$ sample is only an aliquot taken from the $250 \, \text{cm}^{3}$ flask, so consider what factor you must multiply by to get back to the total.
walkthrough:
Picture the volumetric flask**
You dissolved all the soluble iron from the ore and made it up to $250 \, \text{cm}^{3}$, but you only titrated $25.0 \, \text{cm}^{3}$. That means the flask holds ten times what you titrated.

Multiply by the scaling factor**
$$\text{factor} = \frac{250}{25.0} = 10$$ $$n(\text{Fe}^{2+} \text{ in flask}) = 3.28 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 = 3.28 \times 10^{-2} \, \text{mol}$$

hints: Work out $M_{r}$ of $\text{FeCO}_{3}$ by adding the relative atomic masses of one Fe, one C and three O atoms.
Recall that each mole of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in the flask came from one mole of $\text{FeCO}_{3}$, so use mass equals moles times $M_{r}$ with your answer from (iii).
walkthrough:
Calculate $M_{r}$ of iron(II) carbonate**
Add the atoms carefully: $$M_{r} = 55.8 + 12.0 + (3 \times 16.0) = 115.8$$ No brackets to miss here, just one Fe, one C and three O.

Link $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ moles to $\text{FeCO}_{3}$ mass**
Dissolving $\text{FeCO}_{3}$ in excess HCl gives one $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ per formula unit, so $n(\text{FeCO}_{3}) = n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 3.28 \times 10^{-2} \, \text{mol}$. Then: $$m = n \times M_{r} = 3.28 \times 10^{-2} \times 115.8 \approx 3.79 \, \text{g}$$

Final answer: $M_{r}(\text{FeCO}_{3}) = 55.8 + 12.0 + 3(16.0) = 115.8$
mass = $3.28 \times 10^{-2} \times 115.8 = 3.79$ g (3.80 g with full precision)

hints: Recall percentage means mass of pure substance divided by total sample mass times 100, using the original $5.00$ g sample.
walkthrough:
Express the pure mass as a fraction of the ore**
You found about $3.79 \, \text{g}$ of $\text{FeCO}_{3}$ inside a $5.00 \, \text{g}$ sample of spathose. The rest is impurity that was filtered off.

hints: Strip out the spectator chloride ions and focus only on the change: $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ to $\text{Sn}^{4+}$.
Balance electrons by remembering $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ gains one electron while $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ loses two electrons, so you need two iron ions for each tin ion.
walkthrough:
Identify what is oxidised and reduced**
$\text{Fe}^{3+}$ becomes $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ by gaining one electron, so it is reduced. $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ becomes $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ by losing two electrons, so it is oxidised. Chloride ions appear on both sides as $\text{SnCl}_{2}$, $\text{FeCl}_{3}$ etc, so they are spectators and are omitted from the ionic equation.

Balance atoms and charge**
To balance the two electrons lost by tin, you need two iron(III) ions: $$2\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+} + \text{Sn}^{4+}$$ Check charge: left $2(+3)+(+2)=+8$, right $2(+2)+(+4)=+8$. Balanced with no state symbols as requested.

hints: Start with the tin species $\text{SnCl}_{2}$ reacting to form $\text{SnCl}_{4}$, then count Hg and Cl atoms to find how many $\text{HgCl}_{2}$ molecules are needed to make $\text{Hg}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$.
Decide state symbols by remembering all chlorides in solution are (aq) while the white $\text{Hg}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$ is described as a precipitate, so it must be (s).
walkthrough:
Balance the formula equation**
Tin(II) is oxidised to tin(IV): $\text{SnCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{SnCl}_{4}$. The product $\text{Hg}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$ contains two Hg atoms, so you need two $\text{HgCl}_{2}$ on the left. Check Cl: left $2 + 2(2) = 6$, right $4 + 2 = 6$. Balanced: $$\text{SnCl}_{2} + 2\text{HgCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{SnCl}_{4} + \text{Hg}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}$$

Add correct state symbols**
Both tin chlorides and mercury(II) chloride are in aqueous solution, so they are (aq). Mercury(I) chloride forms a white precipitate, so it is a solid: $$\text{SnCl}_{2}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{HgCl}_{2}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{SnCl}_{4}(\text{aq}) + \text{Hg}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2}(\text{s})$$
